The problem is proportion and duplication: about eighty percent of the text is GPU-serving configuration that is recoverable if wrong, while the two genuinely irreversible or proof-threatening items (the pre-ratification egress boundary, and the Tester's permitted adaptation after a language change) get a paragraph and a sentence respectively, and the central unanswered question — whether $300 and a rewrite reach an admissible commit when seven prior attempts did not — is filed as an open question rather than argued. Collapse the triple-stated gate lists into one table, publish an exhaustive supersession index against every Python/Ollama clause in the ratified set, and give the two irreversible edges the same instrument rigor the inherited threat model already mandates.

findings.title: Amendment edits spec/architecture.md §1 by quoting a replacement sentence that does not match the current text
findings.detail: The amendment says 'Replace the first sentence of `spec/architecture.md` section 1 with:' and then quotes a two-sentence block ('The implementation is a Rust 1.98.1 workspace... It uses one canonical event/projection protocol but never one universal graph.'). But architecture.md §1's actual first sentence is 'The implementation is a Python 3.12 package with a CLI and local HTTP service.' — the second sentence ('It uses one canonical event/projection protocol...') is a *separate existing* sentence. So the instruction, executed literally, produces a duplicated sentence. A reader trying to apply this amendment byte-for-byte cannot tell whether to replace one sentence or two, and this is a spec whose own rules say 'exact-byte ratification' and 'Any digest/value disagreement blocks dispatch'.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'Replace the first sentence of `spec/architecture.md` section 1 with: > The implementation is a Rust 1.98.1 workspace, edition 2024, ... It uses one canonical event/projection protocol but never one universal graph.' vs architecture.md §1: 'The implementation is a Python 3.12 package with a CLI and local HTTP service. It uses one canonical event/projection protocol but never one universal graph.'
findings.recommendation: State the exact bytes being removed and the exact bytes replacing them (old/new pair), or say 'replace the first two sentences'. Given the ratification regime, every supersession clause should quote both sides verbatim.

findings.title: Python-specific bindings elsewhere in the ratified specs are not superseded, leaving contradictions a reader cannot resolve
findings.detail: The amendment claims to supersede 'only the clauses named below' and that everything unnamed 'remains byte-for-byte binding'. But at least three unnamed Python-dependent statements survive and now conflict with a Rust workspace: (a) architecture.md §4 adapter `repo_code`: 'language-agnostic files plus Python/TypeScript declarations' — is Python declaration parsing still required in Rust? (b) architecture.md §1: 'The existing Kindex package is integrated behind `PersonalKindexAdapter`... Adapters use public Store/export/import surfaces or subprocess JSON contracts' and 'The preregistration pins Kindex 0.36.0' with `kin export`/`kin ingest` seams — Kindex is a Python package, so a Rust binary must shell out; but §2.1 says 'Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency.' Those two statements cannot both be true if Personal storage runs through a Python `kin` CLI. (c) verification.md role line for Coder is superseded, but the same file's 'Python package installs in a clean environment' is superseded while nothing addresses the Kindex dependency in the nonfunctional gates.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency.' vs architecture.md §1: 'The preregistration pins Kindex 0.36.0. Verified public seams are `kin export` (JSON/JSONL and audience scope), `kin ingest` ... `kin setup-hooks --dry-run` ...' and §6 Personal: '`PersonalKindexAdapter` owns a Kindex SQLite data directory'.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit clause resolving the Kindex/Python boundary: either (i) subprocess invocation of the pinned Kindex CLI is declared outside 'production paths' and named as a permitted external dependency with its own pin, or (ii) the Kindex seam is reimplemented and the §1 seam-conformance clause is superseded. Also state whether `repo_code` Python-declaration parsing remains required.

findings.title: Budget arithmetic makes the stated ceiling look unreachable, and the reader has no way to check the founder's assumption
findings.detail: USD 300 total at 'at most USD 34.01 per hour' is under 8.8 hours of instance time. The amendment separately requires staging a 755.7 GB checkpoint (which counts against the ceiling), a synthetic tool-loop probe, a BF16 KV capacity probe, a forced-interruption resume probe, and then authoring a complete Rust reimplementation of a 29-module system whose Python attempt was 9,378 lines and failed seven times. Assumption 3 is flagged 'Load-bearing' but the reader is given no evidence, no download-time estimate, and no worked example. A first-time reader cannot tell whether this is a plausible plan or a plan that terminates at the USD 285 stop before any Coder turn. The document itself half-admits this in open question 5, but the gate is set at the USD 210 warning — i.e. after ~70% of the budget is already spent.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'The founder authorized USD 300 of available Vast credit... at most USD 34.01 per hour... warns the founder no later than USD 210 consumed, and must stop new Coder turns at USD 285'. §5.3: 'Load-bearing: the remaining USD 300 ceiling is enough to stage, qualify, and produce a coherent Rust candidate.' §1: 'The current 29-module, 9,378-line Python tree remains uncommitted and unadmitted.'
findings.recommendation: Publish the worked hour budget: expected download hours at a stated bandwidth, expected probe hours, and residual Coder hours, with the arithmetic shown. If residual Coder time is under some threshold, say so explicitly and record it as an accepted risk rather than leaving the reader to compute 300/34.01.

findings.title: 'Synthetic probe text and generic Codex harness metadata' is the whole pre-ratification allowlist but is never defined or made checkable
findings.detail: §0 makes this the single load-bearing gate against the irreversible disclosure edge, and failure mode 7 makes violation 'negative V-3 evidence' that 'blocks the run'. But nothing defines what counts as 'generic Codex harness metadata'. Codex harness metadata plausibly includes cwd, repo name, git remote, branch name, user/host name, tool schemas — several of which are repository-derived. A user following this document in good faith could send `cwd=/Users/founder/guildhall` in a routine harness handshake and only later discover it was a run-blocking V-3 failure. There is no enumeration, no detector, and no operator-visible check named.
findings.evidence: §0: 'Synthetic probe text and generic Codex harness metadata are the only pre-ratification request content allowed.' §3.7: 'Non-synthetic or repository-derived prompt/tool output reaches the unratified host... This is negative V-3 evidence and blocks the run; later deletion cannot retroactively authorize it.'
findings.recommendation: Enumerate the exact permitted metadata fields (closed list), name the mechanism that enforces it (egress digest capture already exists in threat-model.md's 'records every outbound model-request digest'), and state what an operator runs to verify compliance before and after each probe.

findings.title: Blindness rules for the Tester are stated as a goal with no enforcement mechanism or failure disposition
findings.detail: §2.3 permits the Tester to 'adapt only language-dependent build/launch plumbing while remaining blind to Rust code'. In practice, adapting a launcher for a Rust workspace requires knowing binary name, target dir layout, cargo invocation, exit-code plumbing, and probably the CLI surface. There is no stated boundary between 'launch plumbing' and 'Rust code', no named reviewer of the diff, and no stated consequence if the boundary is crossed. Compare §2.4 and the failure modes, which are specific about who blocks and what receipt is retained. Open question 4 acknowledges the risk but defers it to 'Validator/Detector inspection' without saying what test distinguishes a compliant amendment from a contaminating one.
findings.evidence: §2.3: 'The Tester may receive this ratified amendment and adapt only language-dependent build/launch plumbing while remaining blind to Rust code'. §5.4: 'Load-bearing: the Tester suite's behavioral oracle can be made language-neutral without reading implementation'. §8.4: 'Can the existing Tester artifact remain behaviorally valid after only an implementation-blind launcher amendment?'
findings.recommendation: Name the permitted change surface concretely (e.g. 'only the process-launch adapter file and its fixtures; assertions and expectations frozen by digest'), require the pre/post digest of the assertion set to be identical, and state the disposition when it is not (fresh Tester generation).

findings.title: Composite-execution attribution string is mandated but the surface it appears on is unspecified
findings.detail: The amendment requires the run to 'say `GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt`'. A reader has no idea where: the evidence packet? the behavior ledger? the sanitized public report? a CLI output? verification.md's evidence-packet list has a 'Coder/Tester/Orchestrator/Validator identities and method limitations' bullet, which is the plausible home, but the amendment never says so. An honest-attribution requirement that names no artifact cannot be checked.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The new run must say `GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt`; it may not claim one uninterrupted thread or one unchanged runtime.'
findings.recommendation: Bind the string to a named field in a named artifact (e.g. the evidence packet's identities/limitations section and the sanitized report header), so its absence is a mechanical failure.

findings.title: The old Python tree's permitted use is stated in two ways that a reader will read as contradictory
findings.detail: §2.2 says the old tree 'may be read only by the new GLM-5.3 Coder as same-role, unadmitted historical work'. But §2.3 and §4 keep the invariant that 'The Rust Coder cannot read tests or Tester findings'. The 9,378-line Python tree was written by a Coder that had already read the same specs — but did it contain test files, fixtures, or expectations? The amendment never says whether the historical tree is scanned for Tester-derived content before the new Coder is allowed to read it. Assumption 5 asserts it 'carries no hidden Tester information' but marks this as a non-load-bearing assumption with no resolution gate, unlike assumptions 1, 2, and 4.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The old Python tree may be read only by the new GLM-5.3 Coder'. §5.5: 'The old Python product is useful same-role translation evidence but carries no hidden Tester information and no authority beyond the specs.' §5 closing: gates are named for assumptions 1, 2, 3, and 4 — 5 and 6 get none.
findings.recommendation: Either promote assumption 5 to load-bearing with a stated resolution gate (a Validator scan of the historical tree for test/fixture/expectation content, receipt retained), or state explicitly which subtree is exposed and that it was verified test-free.

findings.title: The 'fifteen minutes of material changed state' checkpoint rule has no defined measurement or enforcement
findings.detail: The recovery clause says the Coder 'never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint'. 'Material' is undefined, the clock start is undefined, and nothing says who observes the violation or what happens on breach. Failure mode 9 blocks dispatch on a synthetic interruption proof, but that proves survival of *completed events*, not adherence to the fifteen-minute rule during the real run.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The Coder makes a local Git checkpoint after each independently coherent implementation slice and never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint.'
findings.recommendation: Either make it observable (Validator monitors worktree-dirty duration; breach is a recorded finding) or restate it as a Coder instruction rather than an invariant, so a reader knows it is guidance not a gate.

findings.title: No stated disposition for the case where infrastructure probes pass but ratification is then withheld
findings.detail: §0 permits public model staging before ratification. §2.5 notes 'Stopping preserves chargeable storage'. But a running/stopped 8xH200 instance with 755.7 GB staged that never gets ratified will burn the same credit that assumption 3 depends on. The document does not say what happens to a staged instance if the founder or Validator declines ratification, or how long staging may sit before it must be destroyed.
findings.evidence: §0: 'public model staging may precede ratification'. §2.5: 'Stopping preserves chargeable storage; terminal cleanup destroys the instance and retains only local launch, model-manifest, usage, and destruction receipts.'
findings.recommendation: Add a maximum pre-ratification staging window and a mandatory destroy-on-non-ratification clause with its receipt, so credit cannot be consumed by an unratified instance indefinitely.

findings.title: The amendment does not state how a reader determines its own ratification status
findings.detail: The header says 'candidate; not authority; no Coder dispatch permitted from these bytes' and §4 requires 'exact founder and Validator ratification'. But nothing tells a newcomer where the ratification receipt lives or what the ratified digest would be compared against. verification.md says 'the founder may propose amended intent and a distinct Validator may co-ratify exact superseding bytes' but names no ledger location. behavior-ledger.md tracks BL rows, not amendments.
findings.evidence: Header: 'Status: candidate; not authority; no Coder dispatch permitted from these bytes'. §4: 'No repository byte reaches Vast before exact founder and Validator ratification.'
findings.recommendation: Name the artifact and field where the amendment's ratified digest and both signatures are recorded, so anyone holding these bytes can mechanically determine whether they are authority.

persona_reports.summary: Overall: the amendment is unusually disciplined about custody, honest failure semantics, and role isolation — the Factory boundaries, provider-custody language, and the "infrastructure qualification is not Product proof" stance in constraint §4 and failure modes 1–3 all survive intact, and I found no place where a Product behavior, the three-store physical boundary, or a proof gate is quietly weakened. The friction is almost entirely in *executability by a reader*: the §2.1 replacement instruction does not match the text it claims to replace, the "no Python in production paths" clause collides with the still-binding Kindex 0.36.0 Python seam, and the budget arithmetic (300 ÷ 34.01 ≈ 8.8 hours, minus a 755.7 GB download and four probes) is presented as a load-bearing assumption with no worked example. A first-time reader would get stuck applying the amendment to architecture.md, and would not be able to tell whether assumption 3 is credible.

findings.title: Amendment does not supersede architecture.md §1's Python-specific enforcement primitives, leaving the three-store physical boundary under-specified for Rust
findings.detail: The three-store physical boundary in `architecture.md` §1 and §6 is not merely 'Python 3.12 package' prose; it names concrete OS-enforcement mechanisms that the amendment leaves untouched while replacing the runtime that implements them. §5 requires `fexecve`/`execveat` descriptor-backed classifier execution; §6 requires the launcher to open the Personal root as a directory file descriptor only in the Personal worker, to enumerate live descriptors via 'the platform-native facility', to `fstat` each descriptor and reject any whose dev/inode falls under the Personal root, and to enforce a frozen `CLOEXEC`-by-default allowlist. The amendment says only that 'the host process owns Personal capture and launches shared projection/publication as a separately sandboxed child mode with only staged minimum capabilities' and that filesystem locking uses 'maintained Rust crates behind Guildhall-owned interfaces'. It never restates who owns descriptor enumeration/attestation, `fexecve`, macOS `sandbox_init`, or Landlock/bubblewrap in a Rust process model. Worse, the amendment introduces a new architectural claim — 'one deployable package with internal modules' — but §1's enforcement depends on a *multi-process* launcher/Personal-worker/shared-child split with distinct capability sets. 'One deployable binary, several process modes' is compatible; 'one package, internal modules' invites a reviewer or Coder to read the boundary as intra-process module privacy, which is exactly the failure mode failure-mode 4 warns about ('recreates one universal store'). The amendment asserts the boundary is preserved without binding the Rust mechanism that preserves it.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'The workspace is deliberately one deployable package with internal modules, not a service or crate per noun.' and 'the host process owns Personal capture and launches shared projection/publication as a separately sandboxed child mode with only staged minimum capabilities'. Compare `architecture.md` §6 Personal: 'The shared process enumerates its live descriptors using the platform-native facility, rejects any descriptor whose `fstat` device/inode falls under the Personal root... The launcher independently attests the same allowlist.' and §5: 'executes that same descriptor with `fexecve`/`execveat`; it never re-resolves the pathname between check and execution. A platform without verified descriptor-backed execution disables the external-classifier path.'
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit clause to §2.1 stating that the Rust binary retains the three distinct process roles (launcher, Personal worker, shared projector/publisher child) with distinct OS capability sets, and that `fexecve`/`execveat`, descriptor enumeration/`fstat` dev-inode rejection, `CLOEXEC` allowlist attestation, macOS sandbox profile, and Landlock/bubblewrap backends are Guildhall-owned first-party code, not delegated to a convenience crate. State that Rust type-level distinctness of `PersonalStore`/`CompanyStore`/`CodebaseStore` handles is *additional* to, and never a substitute for, the OS/process boundary, and that if the Rust implementation cannot demonstrate descriptor non-possession under V-3 mutation, shared projection disables per §1's existing rule.

findings.title: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in all first-party crates is incompatible with the ratified V-3 descriptor/fexecve/sandbox obligations
findings.detail: The amendment states `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in first-party crates *and* that filesystem locking, etc. use 'maintained Rust crates behind Guildhall-owned interfaces so dependency choice cannot redefine a protocol or trust boundary.' These two statements are in tension with the ratified architecture. `fexecve`/`execveat`, `sandbox_init` (macOS, deprecated C API), Landlock ruleset syscalls, `bubblewrap` argument construction, and directory-descriptor `fstat` enumeration all require `unsafe` FFI somewhere. `forbid` (unlike `deny`) cannot be locally overridden with `#[allow]`, so the only way to satisfy both statements is to push every one of those primitives into a third-party crate — which directly contradicts 'dependency choice cannot redefine a protocol or trust boundary', because the Personal-root descriptor denial *is* the trust boundary per `threat-model.md` catalog item 19 and V-3's 'Pass an open Personal directory descriptor while pathname denial still succeeds; descriptor enumeration/attestation must fail startup'. The amendment has, without saying so, either (a) delegated a Type-1 safety boundary to unvetted crates, or (b) made the ratified boundary unimplementable. Neither is acceptable under the precedence rule `Architecture > Verification` in verification.md.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'sets `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in first-party crates' ... 'SQLite, Ed25519, SHA-256, canonical serialization, filesystem locking, loopback HTTP, and CLI parsing use maintained Rust crates behind Guildhall-owned interfaces so dependency choice cannot redefine a protocol or trust boundary.' Against `threat-model.md` attack 19 and V-3: 'Swap the classifier pathname after descriptor hashing and before execution; only the already verified descriptor may execute.'
findings.recommendation: Replace the blanket `forbid` with a named exception: `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in all first-party crates except one explicitly enumerated `guildhall-os-boundary` crate that owns every syscall implementing the ratified capability boundary, which uses `#![deny(unsafe_code)]` with individually documented, reviewed `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` sites. Require that crate to be first-party (not a dependency), and require the V-3 mutation suite to target it. Record its unsafe-block inventory in the nonfunctional gate rather than asserting a global zero.

findings.title: Amendment silently narrows the Coder's readable authority set, omitting the Acceptance Threat Model from the ratified role line
findings.detail: The replacement Coder role line in §2.2 lists 'the newly ratified product, architecture, threat model, verification strategy, this amendment, and its build lane' — good. But the *original* ratified line in verification.md reads 'reads ratified product, architecture, verification strategy, and its build lane' with no threat model. The amendment therefore *widens* Coder read access to include `threat-model.md`. That is a substantive change to role isolation, presented as if it were incidental language cleanup for the model/host swap. It matters: `threat-model.md` §'Frozen attack catalog' enumerates all nineteen attack families that V-3 will execute, and §'Canary and auxiliary-corpus custody' describes the canary registry structure and planted-surface taxonomy. Giving the Coder the frozen attack catalog is functionally giving the Coder a large fraction of the Tester's instrument shape — precisely what the amendment's own §2.3 forbids ('No Tester file, finding, assertion, fixture, or hidden expectation enters the Coder prompt or repository'). The threat model is an *authority* artifact so this may be intentional and defensible, but the amendment neither flags it as a change nor argues it, and the amendment's own preamble claims it 'supersedes only the clauses named below' while 'Every ... role boundary ... not named here remains byte-for-byte binding.'
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2 replacement: 'reads the newly ratified product, architecture, threat model, verification strategy, this amendment, and its build lane'. Original `verification.md` Role separation: '**Coder (GLM-5.3 via Ollama-launched Codex):** reads ratified product, architecture, verification strategy, and its build lane'. Amendment §2.3: 'No Tester file, finding, assertion, fixture, or hidden expectation enters the Coder prompt or repository.'
findings.recommendation: Either (a) drop `threat model` from the replacement Coder line to preserve the ratified boundary byte-for-byte, or (b) call the widening out explicitly as a named superseded clause, justify why the frozen attack catalog is implementation authority rather than Tester instrument, and state what the Coder must build to satisfy it. If (b), also state whether the Coder sees the attack-catalog digest binding or only the prose, and confirm the Detector Reviewer's coverage challenge is unaffected.

findings.title: Amendment does not resolve which document is authority for Kindex integration once Python is removed, leaving P-1/P-9 potentially unachievable
findings.detail: `architecture.md` §1 pins Kindex 0.36.0 and lists verified public seams (`kin export`, `kin ingest`, `kin setup-hooks --dry-run`, Store node/edge/candidate/verify/invalidate/supersede methods) integrated behind `PersonalKindexAdapter`/`CodebaseKindexAdapter`. Kindex is, by every indication in the spec ('The existing Kindex package', `kin` CLI, 'Store ... methods'), a Python package. The amendment says 'Kindex integration remains through public CLI/library contracts, never direct writes to Kindex SQLite internals' and, separately, 'Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency.' If the Store node/edge/candidate methods are a *library* surface, that is a Python library, and the two statements are contradictory. If Rust must reach Kindex only via `kin` subprocess CLI, then the ratified 'Store node/edge/candidate/verify/invalidate/supersede methods' seam is no longer available and the frozen seam-conformance suite in §1 and §11 cannot be satisfied byte-for-byte — which `architecture.md` says 'blocks P-1/P-2/P-9 proof dispatch'. Either way the amendment has changed a load-bearing integration contract without naming it. Note also that a `kin` subprocess is a Python interpreter in the *proof* path even if not in the shipped 'production package', so §2.1's claim needs a scope qualifier.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'Kindex integration remains through public CLI/library contracts, never direct writes to Kindex SQLite internals' and 'Production paths contain no Python interpreter or Python package dependency.' Against `architecture.md` §1: 'Verified public seams are `kin export` ... and Store node/edge/candidate/verify/invalidate/supersede methods.' and 'Failure is a loud degraded product state and blocks P-1/P-2/P-9 proof dispatch'.
findings.recommendation: Add a §2.1 clause naming the Kindex seam disposition explicitly: state whether Rust reaches Kindex through the `kin` CLI subprocess JSON contract only (and if so, supersede the `Store ... methods` library seam and state how the equivalent verify/invalidate/supersede operations are performed and how the frozen conformance suite is re-expressed), and qualify the no-Python claim as 'no Python in the first-party Guildhall build or shipped artifact; the pinned Kindex 0.36.0 interpreter remains an external subprocess dependency of the proof environment and is recorded in the artifact receipt.'

findings.title: SessionStart p95 and fsck budgets are treated as automatically preserved, but they were calibrated against a different runtime and a different recorded proof machine
findings.detail: The amendment asserts 'the existing CLI names, JSON envelopes, error codes, exit codes, and observable Product behavior remain unchanged unless this amendment explicitly says otherwise.' V-9 requires 200 invocations per host/state on 'the recorded proof machine' with every state's p95 under two seconds, a 250 ms Company connect budget, and full fsck at the 10,000-event ceiling within 120 seconds; V-4 requires the same 120 s revocation cascade bound. These are observable behavior *thresholds*, and a Rust rewrite plausibly makes them easier — but the load-bearing point is that the proof machine record and the measured baselines were produced (or were to be produced) under the Python runtime. The amendment does not state whether prior nonfunctional measurements are void, whether the proof machine is unchanged, or whether the thresholds are re-measured from zero. Silence here creates a real risk that a favorable Rust number is compared against a Python-era record, or that a Python-era 'recorded proof machine' attestation is reused, which is exactly the kind of cross-generation evidence mixing the preamble forbids ('it does not ... retroactively admit any artifact').
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'the existing CLI names, JSON envelopes, error codes, exit codes, and observable Product behavior remain unchanged'. Against `verification.md` V-9: 'run at least 200 invocations per host/state on the recorded proof machine, report CPU/RAM/filesystem, and require every state's p95 under two seconds' and §Preamble: 'Ratification creates a new run generation; it does not rewrite the original manifest or retroactively admit any artifact.'
findings.recommendation: State in §2.1 that all V-4/V-9 latency, throughput, and ceiling measurements are re-executed from zero under the Rust artifact on a newly attested proof machine, that no Python-generation performance receipt is admissible in the new generation's evidence packet, and that the machine attestation is bound into the new manifest.

findings.title: Prefix caching with 'SHA-256/CBOR keys' is asserted as safe but is repository-content-derived state on the provider host, contradicting the custody clause
findings.detail: §2.2 enables vLLM prefix caching with SHA-256/CBOR keys and asserts it 'is neither a result journal nor recovery evidence' and that 'No repository-bearing prompt, response, or result cache is persisted on the Vast host.' Two problems. First, a prefix cache is by construction a cache of repository-bearing prompt content in GPU/host memory (and, in some vLLM configurations, CPU-offloaded or disk-backed KV). 'Not persisted' is a claim about durability, but the ratified `threat-model.md` definition of **durable** is broader than disk: 'written to any filesystem, database, Git object, cache, log, retained evidence, service state, remote request, or cross-process/cross-machine channel where a receiver may retain it after the producing operation returns.' A KV prefix cache is explicitly a *cache* and *service state* that a receiver retains after the request returns. Under the ratified definition, prefix cache contents are durable on an unauthorized-for-Personal host. Second, the amendment does not state that CPU offload / disk-backed prefix caching is disabled; vLLM has offload configurations, and enabling prefix caching without pinning that off leaves the disk-persistence claim unenforced. The custody clause 'The host stores public model artifacts only' is then false as written whenever prefix caching holds Coder-lane repository bytes.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'prefix caching enabled with SHA-256/CBOR keys' and 'vLLM prefix caching remains enabled for efficiency, but it is volatile GPU state, is neither a result journal nor recovery evidence, and may disappear with the instance. No repository-bearing prompt, response, or result cache is persisted on the Vast host.' §2.4: 'The host stores public model artifacts only.' Against `threat-model.md`: '**durable** means written to any filesystem, database, ... cache, log, ... service state, remote request, or cross-process/cross-machine channel where a receiver may retain it after the producing operation returns.'
findings.recommendation: Reword to acknowledge that the prefix cache holds Coder-lane repository-derived bytes in host memory and is therefore inside the named data-processor boundary, not outside it. Explicitly pin CPU/disk KV offload and any prefix-cache persistence backend to disabled, and add a pre-dispatch probe that verifies no KV/prefix state is written to host filesystem. Correct §2.4's 'stores public model artifacts only' to 'persists only public model artifacts to disk; Coder-lane bytes exist transiently in host memory and GPU KV within the authorized processor boundary and are destroyed with the instance.'

findings.title: 'Codebase writes ... under the Git common-directory lock' understates the ratified lock keying and worktree contention rule
findings.detail: `architecture.md` §2 specifies that the repository-scoped admission lock is 'an exclusive OS file lock stored in Git's common directory and keyed by certified repository UUID, so every linked worktree contends on the same lock', and that it 'serializes journal generation, event rename, manifest construction, index/cache update, and receipt finalization'. It further requires that 'Journal states and transitions are a closed enum and every transition fsyncs before the next side effect.' The amendment compresses this to 'Codebase writes remain repository-owned content-addressed `.kin/` events, manifests, journals, and receipts under the Git common-directory lock'. Dropping the UUID keying and the enumerated serialized scope invites a Rust implementer to key on the common-directory path (which is what 'Git common-directory lock' most naturally reads as) rather than the certified UUID. That is not equivalent: the ratified design deliberately keys on the *certificate*, not the path, because §2 also says a discovery hint or path is never admission authority. V-4's mutation 'Admit concurrently from two linked worktrees and prove one exclusive lock ... A worktree-local lock mutation must fail' would still catch a worktree-local lock, but would not catch a path-keyed-but-common-dir lock, so the gate does not backstop this omission.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1 bullet 4. Against `architecture.md` §2: 'A repository-scoped admission lock is an exclusive OS file lock stored in Git's common directory and keyed by certified repository UUID, so every linked worktree contends on the same lock.'
findings.recommendation: Restore the full ratified phrasing in the amendment bullet, or delete the bullet entirely and rely on the preamble's 'Every Product behavior ... not named here remains byte-for-byte binding.' A partial restatement is worse than no restatement, because it reads as a superseding narrowing.

findings.title: Infrastructure resolution gates in §8 are framed as run-enabling but two of them are not distinguished from Product proof in the failure-mode/limitation text
findings.detail: The review target asks specifically whether 'Infrastructure qualification is not Product proof' is preserved. §4 does state 'A passing build, translation completion, or model-server health check is not a product or proof milestone', and §3 item 9 correctly makes journal-survival a *dispatch* precondition. But §8 open question 5 — 'Does the first Rust Coder checkpoint indicate that USD 300 is enough? Report elapsed time, remaining credit, and coherent capability coverage at the USD 210 warning threshold' — introduces 'coherent capability coverage' as a reported quantity at a budget checkpoint. That phrase is a capability-progress judgment made by, or reported to, the Validator mid-run, and the amendment does not say who computes it, whether it is derived from Tester-blind material, or that it carries no evidentiary weight. `verification.md` is explicit: 'Implementation complete, service starts, unit green, architecture present, or Factory milestone reached are never product verdicts.' A mid-run 'coherent capability coverage' report risks becoming a de facto partial proof narrative in the evidence packet, or worse, a channel by which the Validator's assessment of what is missing reaches the Coder. Similarly, §5 assumption 3's 'produce a coherent Rust candidate' names a milestone without binding it to a non-proof label.
findings.evidence: Amendment §8.5: 'Report elapsed time, remaining credit, and coherent capability coverage at the USD 210 warning threshold'. Against `verification.md` Verdict semantics: 'Implementation complete, service starts, unit green, architecture present, or Factory milestone reached are never product verdicts.'
findings.recommendation: Define 'coherent capability coverage' as a Validator-computed, spec-referenced checklist of which P-1..P-10 behaviors have any implementation surface, explicitly labeled `METHOD_POC` progress telemetry with no evidentiary standing, computed without reading Tester artifacts, and never returned to the Coder. Add it to the §4 constraint list alongside 'A passing build ... is not a product or proof milestone.'

findings.title: Superseded verification.md Coder role line is quoted inaccurately, so the 'replace' instruction has no exact anchor
findings.detail: §2.2 says 'Replace the Coder role line in `spec/verification.md` with:' and then gives new text. The current line is '**Coder (GLM-5.3 via Ollama-launched Codex):** reads ratified product, architecture, verification strategy, and its build lane; authors implementation and implementation docs only; cannot read Tester work or judge success.' The amendment's replacement also changes 'authors implementation and implementation docs only' to 'authors Rust implementation and implementation docs only'. That is fine, but the amendment nowhere quotes the *old* bytes it is replacing. Given that `verification.md` states 'The experiment manifest is bound to every exact authority artifact digest' and 'Any digest/value disagreement blocks dispatch', and that this whole amendment is premised on exact-byte supersession ('Ratification creates a new run generation'), a supersession instruction that identifies its target only by description ('the Coder role line') rather than by exact old bytes is not mechanically applicable. The same defect applies to §2.1's 'Replace the first sentence of `spec/architecture.md` section 1' (that one is at least positionally unambiguous) and §2.1's 'Replace `spec/verification.md`'s Python-package nonfunctional gate' (the target is the bullet 'Python package installs in a clean environment and commands have bounded help.' — replacing it with a six-line block changes list structure, which the amendment does not address).
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'Replace the Coder role line in `spec/verification.md` with:'. Amendment §2.1: 'Replace `spec/verification.md`'s Python-package nonfunctional gate with:'. Against `verification.md`: 'The experiment manifest is bound to every exact authority artifact digest and may contain only values permitted or deterministically derived by them. Any digest/value disagreement blocks dispatch.'
findings.recommendation: For each of the three replacements, quote the exact superseded bytes verbatim alongside the replacement bytes, and state the resulting document's new SHA-256. Without old-byte anchors, ratification cannot be verified mechanically and the Validator has to adjudicate by preference — which `verification.md` forbids ('no role adjudicates by preference inside the run').

findings.title: Budget ceiling arithmetic leaves no margin for the 755.7 GB staging step, making assumption 3 optimistic rather than load-bearing-tested
findings.detail: §2.5 authorizes USD 300 at up to USD 34.01/hour, giving roughly 8.8 hours total, with a hard stop on new Coder turns at USD 285 (≈8.4 h). §3 item 1 and §2.5 both charge public-weight download against the ceiling. A 755.7 GB FP8 checkpoint pull from Hugging Face to a marketplace instance is commonly 1–3 hours even on good links, and the vLLM image is another ~10–20 GB. Add the pre-dispatch capacity probe (§8.2), the synthetic tool-loop probe (§8.1), and the forced-interruption journal probe (§8.3) — all of which run on the paid instance — and the *remaining* Coder time before the USD 285 stop is plausibly 4–6 hours. §5 assumption 3 calls the ceiling 'load-bearing' and correctly says failure is 'an honest capacity result', which is good. But §8.5 asks the question only at the USD 210 checkpoint, by which point roughly 6.2 h are gone; if 3 h went to staging and probes, the first checkpoint arrives with ~2.2 h of Coder work done and ~2.2 h remaining. The amendment does not require a pre-dispatch estimate of staging + probe cost against the ceiling, so the founder cannot make an informed pre-spend decision.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.5: 'USD 300 of available Vast credit ... at most USD 34.01 per hour. The Validator warns the founder no later than USD 210 consumed, and must stop new Coder turns at USD 285'; 'Public-weight download, runtime smoke tests, and failed admitted Coder turns count against the ceiling.' §5.3: 'the remaining USD 300 ceiling is enough to stage, qualify, and produce a coherent Rust candidate.'
findings.recommendation: Add a §2.5 pre-dispatch gate: before the first repository-bearing prompt, the Validator records actual staging + probe spend and the resulting remaining Coder hours, and reports them to the founder. If remaining Coder budget is below a founder-ratified floor, the run terminates as an honest capacity result before any repository byte is transmitted, preserving the irreversible-disclosure edge unspent. Consider whether staging can be done once and snapshotted so a lost instance does not re-charge the full download.

findings.title: 'Local Codex tool execution' plus 'Vast host runs inference only' does not address tool-call arguments as an egress channel
findings.detail: §2.2 says 'local Codex tool execution in the isolated Coder repository. The Vast host runs inference only and receives no repository clone, filesystem mount, credentials, tests, Kindex graph, or coordination channel.' The Codex harness loop is: the model *emits* a tool call, the local harness executes it, and the local harness *sends the result back* to the model. So the Vast host receives (a) the system prompt and every prior turn, (b) every tool result the harness returns, and (c) the model's own generated code. §2.4 acknowledges (b) partially — 'sends only its prompt plus selected Coder-lane tool results' — but §2.2's 'runs inference only and receives no ... tests, Kindex graph' is misleading if the Coder can issue an arbitrary `read_file` or `grep` in its repository. The isolation depends entirely on what is *present in the Coder worktree*, not on the tool-execution locality. This is correctly gated by §2.3's Tester/Coder lane separation and §4's 'The Rust Coder cannot read tests or Tester findings', but the amendment never says the Coder worktree is *materially* free of Tester artifacts, Kindex graph data, and Personal/Company store fixtures — it only says the Coder cannot read them, which is a policy statement, not a filesystem statement. `verification.md` is honest about this: 'Because this is not kernel-enforced isolation, that audit limits the method claim even when clean.' The amendment should inherit that honesty rather than assert host-side absence.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'The Vast host runs inference only and receives no repository clone, filesystem mount, credentials, tests, Kindex graph, or coordination channel.' Against `verification.md` Role separation: 'Coder and Tester use disjoint worktrees and prompts. The Validator audits filesystem access/logs for cross-lane reads. Because this is not kernel-enforced isolation, that audit limits the method claim even when clean.'
findings.recommendation: Add: the Coder worktree is a materially separate checkout containing no Tester lane, no hidden test, no canary registry, no Personal/Company store root, and no Kindex data directory, verified by a pre-dispatch inventory receipt. Restate §2.2 as 'the Vast host receives only what the local harness sends: the prompt, prior turns, and tool results drawn from the Coder worktree; host-side absence of Tester and store material follows from worktree composition and the Validator's cross-lane read audit, not from inference-only hosting', and inherit verification.md's non-kernel-enforcement caveat.

findings.title: Composite-execution attribution string is required but no clause forbids the Ollama/Python generation's evidence from entering the new evidence packet
findings.detail: §2.2 requires the run to say 'GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt', and §3 item 8 blocks contamination of 'attribution or ... the shipped product'. §4 requires the packet to contain 'Coder/Tester/Orchestrator/Validator identities and method limitations'. What is missing is the converse rule: `verification.md`'s evidence packet lists 'all failed attempts' as required content, and the Python generation is a failed attempt of a *different generation* under a *different manifest digest*. The amendment's preamble says ratification 'does not rewrite the original manifest or retroactively admit any artifact' — good — but does not say whether the new generation's packet must include, may include, or must exclude the prior generation's receipts. Since the seven Ollama terminations produced no admissible Coder commit, including them as 'failed attempts' would be honest; excluding them silently would understate the composite. The amendment leaves this to interpretation at exactly the point where honest failure semantics matter most.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'The new run must say `GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt`; it may not claim one uninterrupted thread or one unchanged runtime.' Against `verification.md` Evidence packet: 'all failed attempts and the terminal `PROVEN`, `NOT_PROVEN`, ... verdict'.
findings.recommendation: State that the new generation's evidence packet includes the prior generation's terminal disposition (seven terminations, no admissible commit, uncommitted 29-module/9,378-line tree) as cross-generation method-limitation context bound by digest, explicitly labeled as prior-generation and non-admissible as conformance evidence, and that omitting it is a reporting failure under the same rule that forbids unqualified privacy claims.

findings.title: vLLM 'Responses' endpoint assumption is stated as a compatibility question but not as a specification-version risk
findings.detail: §2.2 pins `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.28.0` and specifies 'a Vast-hosted vLLM Responses endpoint', with §5 assumption 2 covering compatibility and §8 question 1 resolving it by synthetic probe. That is the right shape. What is not addressed: the OpenAI Responses API is a comparatively new and still-evolving surface, and vLLM's implementation of it has historically lagged the Chat Completions path in tool-calling and streaming fidelity. The amendment also independently pins 'GLM-4.7 tool parser, and GLM-4.5 reasoning parser' for a `GLM-5.3` checkpoint — i.e., it is knowingly using parsers named for *different model versions*. That is a plausible engineering reality (parsers are often reused across a family) but it is a stated cross-version assumption that the amendment does not flag as one, and §5 assumption 2 speaks only of 'GLM tool parser' generically without acknowledging the version mismatch. If GLM-5.3's actual tool-call or reasoning envelope differs from GLM-4.7/4.5, the failure mode is silent corruption of tool calls — exactly §3 item 2, but the probe in §8.1 is described as testing 'streamed Responses semantics' rather than parser fidelity across a version gap.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'GLM-4.7 tool parser, and GLM-4.5 reasoning parser' for 'model repository `zai-org/GLM-5.3`'. §5.2: 'vLLM 0.28.0's Responses API and GLM tool parser support the Codex tool loop without corrupting tool calls or reasoning messages.'
findings.recommendation: Promote the parser version gap to an explicit named assumption: 'the GLM-4.7 tool parser and GLM-4.5 reasoning parser correctly parse GLM-5.3's tool-call and reasoning envelopes.' Make §8.1's probe test parser fidelity specifically — multi-call, nested-argument, and reasoning-interleaved cases — not just streamed Responses transport. Add a fallback disposition (Chat Completions path, or a pinned alternative parser) that, like FP8-KV, is a separately recorded configuration change rather than a silent substitution.

findings.title: Fifteen-minute unchecked-work bound is stated without a mechanism that enforces it
findings.detail: §2.2 says the Coder 'never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint.' This is a behavioral instruction to a model, not an enforced invariant. The rest of the amendment is careful about this distinction elsewhere (e.g., §3 item 9 requires a *synthetic interruption proof* before dispatch). §9's dispatch gate proves that completed events survive and the thread resumes, but nothing proves the fifteen-minute bound holds, and nothing detects violation. Given that the amendment's whole recovery story depends on it — 'At most the in-flight model generation may be lost' — an unenforced bound weakens that claim to 'at most fifteen minutes plus the in-flight generation, if the Coder complied.'
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.2: 'The Coder makes a local Git checkpoint after each independently coherent implementation slice and never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint... At most the in-flight model generation may be lost.'
findings.recommendation: Add a local watchdog owned by the Validator (not the Coder) that observes worktree mtime/dirty-state age and either auto-checkpoints or blocks the next Coder turn when the bound is exceeded, and record its receipts. Then restate the recovery claim as bounded by the enforced mechanism rather than by Coder compliance.

findings.title: Rust edition/toolchain pin combination should be stated as internally consistent
findings.detail: §2.1 pins 'Rust 1.98.1 workspace, edition 2024'. Edition 2024 requires a sufficiently recent toolchain; 1.98.1 is a plausible future version but the amendment does not state a minimum supported Rust version separate from the pin, nor whether `rust-toolchain.toml` pins a channel with a hash. `verification.md`'s replacement nonfunctional gate requires recording 'compiler version, target, and binary digest' — good — but a bare version string in `rust-toolchain.toml` resolves to whatever the distribution channel currently serves for that version, which is normally stable but is not a digest-level pin comparable to the vLLM image manifest digest the amendment demands for the model side. The asymmetry is noticeable: the model runtime is pinned by `sha256:`, the compiler is pinned by a version string.
findings.evidence: Amendment §2.1: 'a Rust 1.98.1 workspace, edition 2024' and 'The implementation pins Rust with `rust-toolchain.toml`'. Compare §2.2: '`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.28.0`, manifest digest `sha256:61fc8a...`'.
findings.recommendation: Record the resolved toolchain component checksums (or a container image digest for the build environment) in the artifact receipt, matching the rigor applied to the vLLM image. State the edition-2024 minimum toolchain explicitly so a future rebuild cannot silently succeed on a different compiler.

persona_reports.summary: Overall this is a disciplined, unusually honest amendment: the irreversible-disclosure framing, the pre-ratification synthetic-only rule, the refusal to let infrastructure qualification stand in for Product proof, and the composite-execution attribution requirement are all correct and I would not want them weakened. My blocking concerns are three: (1) the amendment restates the three-store boundary in Rust terms but never binds the Rust process/descriptor/`fexecve` mechanisms that actually enforce it, and its `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` clause is in direct tension with implementing those mechanisms first-party; (2) it silently widens the Coder's readable authority to include the frozen attack catalog, which is a role-isolation change presented as language cleanup; and (3) it leaves the Kindex integration contract ambiguous in a way that could make P-1/P-9 undispatchable once Python leaves the production path. Fix those, quote the exact superseded bytes for each of the three replacements, and correct the prefix-cache custody language against the ratified definition of "durable," and I would sign off.

findings.title: USD 300 buys roughly 8.8 hours on an 8xH200 — the checkpoint download alone can eat a third of it
findings.detail: The amendment authorizes USD 300 at up to USD 34.01/hour. That is 8.82 hours of wall clock, and the amendment explicitly says download, smoke tests, and failed turns all count against it. A 755.7 GB FP8 checkpoint pull from Hugging Face at a realistic 1-3 Gbps sustained marketplace rate is 35 minutes to 1.7 hours — USD 20 to USD 58 before a single token is generated. Add vLLM 0.28.0 image pull, engine startup and CUDA graph capture for TP=8 at 262K context (routinely 10-25 minutes on a large MoE checkpoint, and repeated on every restart), the synthetic tool-loop probe (Open Question 1), the BF16 KV capacity probe (Open Question 2), and the forced-tunnel-interruption journal probe (Open Question 3). Section 2.2 also states that on endpoint loss the Validator restores the same pinned config — meaning another full stage-and-warm cycle, which on a fresh instance means re-downloading 755.7 GB. Realistically you have 4-6 hours of actual Coder generation, and every infrastructure hiccup is a 30-60 minute, USD 20-35 tax. The product being built is a 29-module system whose Python attempt reached 9,378 lines without an admissible commit. The arithmetic does not close.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'The founder authorized USD 300 of available Vast credit... at most USD 34.01 per hour... Public-weight download, runtime smoke tests, and failed admitted Coder turns count against the ceiling.' §2.2: 'official native-FP8 model files (approximately 755.7 GB)'. §2.2: 'On endpoint loss, the Validator restores the same pinned serving configuration'. §1: 'The current 29-module, 9,378-line Python tree remains uncommitted and unadmitted.' Assumption 3 concedes this is load-bearing: 'the remaining USD 300 ceiling is enough to stage, qualify, and produce a coherent Rust candidate.'
findings.recommendation: Before ratification, write down the explicit budget decomposition: download hours, warmup hours per cold start, expected number of cold starts, probe hours, and residual generation hours. If residual generation is under ~5 hours, either (a) raise the ceiling deliberately with eyes open, (b) use a persistent Vast volume or a pre-baked template so a restart does not re-download 755.7 GB, or (c) accept explicitly in writing that the likely outcome of this run is an honest NOT_PROVEN capacity result rather than a Rust candidate, and decide whether USD 300 is worth buying that information. Do not discover this at hour six.

findings.title: 'Stopping preserves chargeable storage' is an open-ended meter with no owner and no cap
findings.detail: §2.5 acknowledges that stopping the instance preserves chargeable storage but assigns no ceiling, no clock, and no responsible party to it. On Vast, 1 TB of container storage on a stopped instance still bills continuously. If the run ends at hour eight in an ambiguous state — partial checkpoint, half-verified probe, founder asleep — the natural human action is 'stop it, I'll look tomorrow.' That decision quietly converts a terminated experiment into an indefinite subscription against the same USD 300 credit pool. The amendment's own terminal-cleanup path (destroy, retain receipts) is correct; the problem is that 'stop' is described as an available state without the corresponding financial guardrail.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'Stopping preserves chargeable storage; terminal cleanup destroys the instance and retains only local launch, model-manifest, usage, and destruction receipts.' No stopped-state ceiling, maximum stopped duration, or named owner appears anywhere in §2.5 or §4.
findings.recommendation: Add a hard rule: the instance may be in stopped state for at most N hours, after which the Validator destroys it unconditionally; and stopped-state storage charges count against the same USD 285 stop threshold. Name the Validator as the party who owns the destroy action, with a wall-clock deadline, not a judgment call.

findings.title: The USD 210 warning and USD 285 stop have no stated latency, alerting mechanism, or unattended behavior
findings.detail: §2.5 says 'The Validator warns the founder no later than USD 210 consumed, and must stop new Coder turns at USD 285 consumed.' At USD 34.01/hour, the window between those two numbers is 2 hours 12 minutes. If the Validator is a process that polls Vast billing every 15 minutes, that is fine. If it is a human reading a dashboard, it fails the 3am test outright: a long Coder generation started at USD 280 can run past USD 300 while nobody is looking, and the amendment gives no defined behavior for 'credit exhausted mid-generation.' Compare with the discipline applied elsewhere in the contract — verification.md's Operational limits require that 'The harness atomically reserves and enforces the aggregate ceiling' for the V-10 benchmark. This amendment asserts a ceiling without specifying the same enforcement class. Additionally, §2.2 says the Coder 'never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint' — if the instance dies from credit exhaustion rather than a controlled stop, you lose up to fifteen minutes of work and, worse, you lose the endpoint with no credit to restore it. That is a terminal state reached by inattention rather than by decision.
findings.evidence: §2.5: 'The Validator warns the founder no later than USD 210 consumed, and must stop new Coder turns at USD 285 consumed unless the founder explicitly raises the ceiling.' Contrast verification.md Operational limits: 'The harness atomically reserves and enforces the aggregate ceiling.' §2.2: 'never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint.'
findings.recommendation: Specify the mechanism and the poll interval: an automated spend check on a stated cadence, what it does when the check itself fails or the billing API is unreachable (fail closed — stop new turns), and the defined disposition when credit exhausts mid-generation. Make 'stop new Coder turns' a mechanical gate the Validator enforces before dispatch, not an intention. If the Validator is a human, state the required attendance window and forbid dispatching a Coder turn when the founder is unreachable and spend is above USD 250.

findings.title: 'The Validator restores the same pinned serving configuration' hides a multi-hour, multi-hundred-dollar recovery you have not costed
findings.detail: The recovery story in §2.2 reads as if endpoint loss is a reconnect. It is not. If the Vast instance itself is lost — preempted, host failure, or an H200 fault, which §3.1 explicitly anticipates — restoration means: acquire a new verified 8xH200 instance at current marketplace availability, pull the vLLM image, re-download 755.7 GB, re-warm the engine, re-establish the SSH tunnel, and re-run the pre-dispatch probes to prove the new node still satisfies the BF16 KV assumption. That is plausibly 1.5-3 hours and USD 50-100, on a USD 300 budget, at whatever hour the failure happens. §3.1 says failure to stage means 'no Coder dispatch occurs; preserve the infrastructure receipt and select a replacement only under the same pinned artifact/runtime class' — but it does not say what happens when this occurs mid-run with USD 90 remaining. The honest answer is 'the run ends,' and the amendment should say so rather than describing restoration as routine.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'On endpoint loss, the Validator restores the same pinned serving configuration and resumes the same local Codex thread. At most the in-flight model generation may be lost.' §3.1: 'the host disappears, or an H200 fails. No Coder dispatch occurs; preserve the infrastructure receipt and select a replacement only under the same pinned artifact/runtime class.' No cost or time is attached to either.
findings.recommendation: Split §2.2's recovery clause into two named cases with explicit cost: (a) tunnel/process loss where the instance survives — cheap reconnect, minutes; (b) instance loss — full re-stage, state the hour and dollar estimate. Add a rule that if remaining credit is below the measured full re-stage cost, the run terminates as an honest capacity result rather than attempting a restore it cannot finish.

findings.title: Nothing mechanically enforces the 'no repository byte reaches Vast' boundary — it is a rule with no gate
findings.detail: This is the amendment's own declared irreversible edge (§0), and §3.7 correctly names its violation as negative V-3 evidence that blocks the run and cannot be retroactively authorized. But the entire enforcement rests on the operator correctly configuring a local Codex harness to send only synthetic content during the pre-ratification window. Codex harnesses read repository context by default. The failure mode is not adversarial — it is a stray `--cd`, a wrong working directory, or a probe script that accidentally reads a real file. And the consequence is exactly the thing §0 calls unprovable-to-erase: 'Once a repository byte is transmitted to a marketplace host, that disclosure cannot be proven erased even if the instance is destroyed.' Note the contrast with the rest of the contract, which is rigorous about this class of problem: architecture.md §5 requires descriptor-backed `fexecve` execution so a pathname cannot be swapped between check and use; §6 requires descriptor enumeration and fstat device/inode checks, not merely pathname denial. Amendment 001 asks for a comparable irreversible-disclosure boundary and supplies only prose.
findings.evidence: §0: 'no byte sourced from the Guildhall repository... may reach the Vast host before this amendment is exactly ratified. Synthetic probe text and generic Codex harness metadata are the only pre-ratification request content allowed.' §4: 'No repository byte reaches Vast before exact founder and Validator ratification.' Compare architecture.md §5: 'it never re-resolves the pathname between check and execution.' No egress gate, request-content scanner, or launch-time repository-isolation attestation is specified anywhere in the amendment.
findings.recommendation: Require, before any pre-ratification probe, that the probe runs from an empty scratch directory with no Guildhall repository on the filesystem, and that every outbound request body digest be logged locally so the transcript can be audited after the fact. Better: make the Vast-facing harness structurally incapable of reading the repository during the probe window — separate machine, separate user, or a container with no repository mount. threat-model.md already demands 'positive controls in the egress detector' for the model-provider boundary; apply the same standard here. A rule that depends on nobody making a routine mistake is not a boundary for something §0 classifies as irreversible.

findings.title: Three load-bearing assumptions must all hold, and the amendment does not order or cost their probes
findings.detail: §5 declares four load-bearing assumptions; three of them (1: BF16 KV at 262K on this node; 2: vLLM 0.28.0 Responses + GLM tool parser with the Codex loop; 4: language-neutral Tester oracle) can each independently kill the run, and §8 adds a fourth gate (journal survival across forced tunnel interruption). §8 says probes 1, 2, and 3 resolve 'before any repository prompt' but does not order them or bound their cost. This matters because the probes have wildly different costs: the tool-loop probe (§8.1) and the journal-interruption probe (§8.3) can largely be run against a cheap endpoint or even a stub, while the BF16 capacity probe (§8.2) requires the full 8xH200 instance warm and therefore burns the expensive meter. If the capacity probe is run first and passes, then the tool-loop probe fails at hour three, you have spent roughly USD 100 discovering an incompatibility that a USD 0 local test would have surfaced. Failure mode 2 says 'A synthetic, repository-free tool round trip must fail before dispatch' — correct — but says nothing about when relative to instance acquisition.
findings.evidence: §5 lists assumptions 1, 2, 3, 4 all as 'Load-bearing.' §8 lists resolution gates 1, 2, 3 each as 'Resolve before any repository prompt' with no ordering. §3.2: 'A synthetic, repository-free tool round trip must fail before dispatch.'
findings.recommendation: Order the gates cheapest-first and say so in the amendment: resolve Assumption 2 (vLLM Responses / GLM tool parser compatibility with the Codex loop) and Open Question 3 (journal survival) against the cheapest available GLM-5.3 endpoint or a local stub before acquiring the 8xH200 instance. Only then acquire the expensive instance and resolve Assumption 1. Attach a spend cap to the probe phase specifically, so a failed probe cannot consume the generation budget.

findings.title: Assumption 4 has no deadline and can strand a completed Rust candidate with no valid instrument
findings.detail: Assumption 4 states that the Tester suite's behavioral oracle can be made language-neutral without reading implementation, 'otherwise independent comparison requires a fresh Tester generation.' §2.3 permits the Tester to 'adapt only language-dependent build/launch plumbing while remaining blind to Rust code.' §8.4 says resolve 'before its admission.' But 'before its admission' is after the Coder run, not before it. That ordering means the plausible bad path is: spend the full USD 300, produce a coherent Rust candidate, then discover the existing Tester artifact is not behaviorally valid for a Rust binary, and now need a fresh Tester generation — which is unbudgeted, unscheduled, and per verification.md must be produced by an implementation-blind agent who cannot look at what you just built. The money is spent and the proof is not closer.
findings.evidence: §5 Assumption 4: 'otherwise independent comparison requires a fresh Tester generation.' §8.4: 'Can the existing Tester artifact remain behaviorally valid after only an implementation-blind launcher amendment? Resolve before its admission.' §2.3: 'The Tester may receive this ratified amendment and adapt only language-dependent build/launch plumbing.' verification.md Role separation confirms the Tester 'cannot read implementation or Coder work.'
findings.recommendation: Move gate 8.4 earlier: have the Validator/Detector inspect the existing Tester artifact for Python-specific implementation coupling immediately after ratification and before the first paid Coder turn. §5 already says 'Assumption 4 is resolved by Validator/Detector inspection without showing results to the Coder' — that inspection costs nothing and needs no Vast instance. Doing it first converts a post-spend surprise into a pre-spend decision.

findings.title: The composite-execution disclosure is stated once and never bound to the evidence packet
findings.detail: §2.2 requires the new run to say 'GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt' and forbids claiming one uninterrupted thread. This is exactly the right honesty rule. But verification.md's Evidence packet enumerates required contents in detail — 'Coder/Tester/Orchestrator/Validator identities and method limitations' — and the amendment does not amend that list to require the composite-execution string, the Ollama failure receipt, or the two-runtime disclosure. Under authority precedence ('Verification > generated manifest'), an unamended verification.md governs packet contents. The risk is not deception; it is that a future reader of the packet reconstructs a cleaner history than actually occurred, because the disclosure lived in an amendment rather than in the artifact that defines what gets recorded. Note that verification.md is already emphatic that the Factory method evidence is labeled METHOD_POC and never CLEAN_QUALIFIED — the same instinct applies here.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The new run must say `GLM-5.3 composite execution: Ollama/Python attempt -> Vast/Rust attempt`; it may not claim one uninterrupted thread or one unchanged runtime.' verification.md Evidence packet: 'Coder/Tester/Orchestrator/Validator identities and method limitations' — no composite-execution or prior-attempt field. §2.1 and §2.2 amend architecture.md §1 and verification.md's Coder role line and Python gate, but not the Evidence packet section.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit clause amending verification.md's Evidence packet to require: the composite-execution string verbatim, the Ollama/Python attempt receipt including its seven terminations, and the historical-evidence location of the unadmitted 9,378-line Python tree. Otherwise the honesty rule depends on whoever assembles the packet remembering an amendment clause.

findings.title: 'Never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state' has no enforcement and no measurement
findings.detail: §2.2 sets a fifteen-minute checkpoint discipline for the Coder, and §3.6 repeats it as the mitigation for running out of credit. Both are stated as obligations on the Coder — an LLM in a Codex thread. There is no watchdog, no timer, no mechanical enforcement, and no defined behavior when the Coder simply does not checkpoint because it is deep in a long generation. On a route where the endpoint can vanish and the budget can exhaust, the fifteen-minute rule is the only thing standing between a lost instance and lost work, and it is enforced by the least reliable party in the system.
findings.evidence: §2.2: 'The Coder makes a local Git checkpoint after each independently coherent implementation slice and never carries more than fifteen minutes of material changed state without a checkpoint.' §3.6: 'The Coder must make small coherent local commits/checkpoints.' No watchdog, timer, or violation disposition is specified.
findings.recommendation: Make it mechanical: a local watchdog on the workstation that commits or stashes the Coder worktree on a timer independent of the Coder's cooperation, or have the Validator's turn-dispatch gate refuse a new Coder turn when the worktree has uncommitted changes older than fifteen minutes. The state you need to survive an outage should not depend on the model choosing to save it.

findings.title: Structural preservation of the contract is genuinely sound — the risk here is operational, not architectural
findings.detail: On the questions the review brief actually asks: the amendment preserves what it claims to preserve. §2.1 restates the three physical stores as 'distinct, non-convertible PersonalStore, CompanyStore, and CodebaseStore handles; no universal store handle and no audience-selecting open operation,' which is a faithful transposition of architecture.md §1's 'The type and runtime interfaces do not offer "select audience" or "open all stores."' §2.3 preserves Factory role isolation exactly — Agy block/no-op only, Coder blind to Tester, Tester blind to implementation, fresh Detector Review required. §2.4 extends threat-model.md's model-provider boundary without weakening it and is admirably honest that 'container isolation is not a confidentiality proof' and that 'Vast's deletion assertion is operational evidence, not proof.' §4's final bullet — 'A passing build, translation completion, or model-server health check is not a product or proof milestone' — directly answers the brief's 'infrastructure qualification is not Product proof' concern, as does §6's refusal to claim memory safety of dependencies or privacy. The append-only supersession model in §7.6 is the right call. My findings are therefore concentrated on operations and money, not on whether the proof was weakened.
findings.evidence: §2.1 store handles; §2.3 role separation; §2.4 custody boundary; §4 final bullet; §6 limitations; §7.6 append-only rationale. Cross-checked against architecture.md §1, threat-model.md 'Model-provider boundary', verification.md 'Role separation' and 'Verdict semantics'.
findings.recommendation: No action on structure. Direct remediation effort at the budget arithmetic (finding 1), the pre-ratification egress boundary (finding 5), and the probe ordering (findings 6 and 7).

persona_reports.summary:
The specification discipline here is unusually good, and the amendment does not smuggle in any weakening of the three-store boundary, the role isolation, or the honest-failure semantics — it is explicit that a green build is not a proof milestone, and that is the right instinct. My concern is not that you'll ship something unsafe; it's that USD 300 at USD 34/hour buys roughly 8.8 hours, of which 755.7 GB of checkpoint download, TP=8 engine warmup, and three pre-dispatch probes will consume a large and uncosted fraction, and a single instance loss forces a full re-stage you have not budgeted for.

The two things I'd fix before ratifying: write the actual hour-by-hour budget decomposition so you know now whether this run can finish, and put a mechanical gate — not a rule in prose — between the Guildhall repository and the Vast host during the pre-ratification probe window, because §0 correctly identifies that disclosure as the one thing you cannot undo. Everything else on my list is a matter of you getting woken up at 3am to babysit a re-download instead of being told, cleanly, that the run ended.
